problem.claim: Reduce MoE inference communication, VRAM demands, and latency while retaining its performance benefits.

gap.claim: Existing MoE deployment requires all experts in VRAM, while expert offloading increases inference latency because experts are loaded only when needed.

contributions.claim: Proposes Mixture of Lookup Experts (MoLE), an MoE architecture designed to reduce communication and VRAM usage.
Uses FFN experts during training and re-parameterizes them into input-id-indexed lookup tables for inference, allowing expert outputs to be retrieved from storage rather than recomputed.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present MoLE as a new MoE architecture that converts trained FFN experts into lookup tables before inference.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that, at matched FLOPs and VRAM usage, MoLE reaches inference speeds comparable to dense models.
The authors report that MoLE is significantly faster than MoE with expert offloading while maintaining performance on par with MoE.

narrative_sequence.summary: MoE scales parameter count while activating only a subset of experts, preserving low inference FLOPs and latency.
Dynamic expert selection still requires all experts in VRAM; offloading reduces this requirement but substantially raises latency.
MoLE trains FFN experts, then converts them into lookup tables whose outputs are retrieved by input id and loaded from storage during inference.
Under matched FLOPs and VRAM usage, the authors report dense-model-comparable speed, faster inference than offloaded MoE, and MoE-level performance.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns a deployment bottleneck with a concrete representation change: trained FFN experts become lookup tables, eliminating inference-time expert computation and making communication overhead negligible.

lessons.interpretation: Separating training-time computation from inference-time retrieval can directly target systems constraints.
lessons.application: When deployment cost is dominated by repeated computation or transfer, consider whether a trained component can be compiled into an indexed representation and evaluate it under matched resource budgets.
lessons.exception: This approach may be unsuitable when inputs are too numerous or continuous for feasible lookup-table storage, or when exact input-id retrieval is unavailable.

unknowns: The abstract gives no latency values, hardware or workload details, statistical variation, or definition of the performance metric.
The storage size and construction cost of the lookup tables are not reported.
The conditions and scope behind the claim of negligible communication overhead are unspecified.
